The compressor was designed and fabricated under a NASA contract with 2/3 funding from NASA and 1/3 from UTRC.
The design target was to increase efficiency at higher work factor while reducing the maximum diameter of the stage.
The compressor achieved a pressure ratio of 4.68, work factor of 0.81, and design exit corrected flow rate of 3 lbm/s.
The measured polytropic efficiency was 85.5% and the stall margin was 7.5% at the design flow rate and speed.
The measured efficiency and stall margin were lower than pre-test CFD predictions by 2.4 percentage points and 4.5 percentage points, respectively.
The impeller had a 30° backsweep and featured 3D aero concepts to improve efficiency.
The diffuser design explored different topologies and splitter vane placements to optimize the impeller-diffuser interaction.
Detailed structural analyses were conducted on the impeller, shroud, diffuser, and exit guide vanes to ensure structural integrity.
Post-test analyses identified unsteady impeller-diffuser interactions, flow-rate mismatch, and flow separation in the radial-to-axial bend as the key reasons for the lower-than-predicted performance.
The authors recommended redesigning the diffuser and radial-to-axial bend to address the identified issues.
The authors identified limitations in the implementation of turbulence models and the need for longer integration times in unsteady CFD simulations.
The authors proposed testing the impeller with a vaneless diffuser to better understand the impeller-diffuser interactions.
The compressor was designed to fit within the existing Small Engine Components Test Facility at NASA Glenn Research Center.
The fabrication process encountered some challenges, including issues with the impeller that were resolved.
The compressor was successfully installed and tested at the NASA Glenn Research Center facility.
